structure.title: I
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway, Nick Carraway, reflecting on his father's advice to reserve judgment, a habit that made him a confidant in college and shaped his moral outlook, though he later became disillusioned by the moral chaos he witnessed in the East—except for Gatsby, whom he uniquely admired for his extraordinary gift for hope. In the spring of 1922, Nick rents a modest eighty-dollar bungalow in West Egg, arriving alone after his roommate is sent to Washington; he feels isolated until a stranger asks him for directions, granting him a sense of belonging. That evening, he drives by car to East Egg to dine with his cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, a Yale acquaintance, at their grand Georgian Colonial mansion, where he meets the enigmatic Jordan Baker, who lies motionless on a couch. During dinner, Tom aggressively espouses racist pseudoscience from 'The Rise of the Coloured Empires,' and a telephone call reveals his affair with a woman in New York, which Jordan confirms to Nick; Daisy, visibly shaken, deflects with a fabricated story about a nightingale and later confesses her despair, wishing her daughter would be a 'beautiful little fool.' After dinner, in the crimson-lit living room, Jordan reads from the Saturday Evening Post and announces bedtime, while Daisy jokes about marrying Nick to Jordan, which Tom disapproves of sarcastically; Daisy and Tom interrogate Nick about rumors of his engagement to a woman out West, unsettling him with their intrusive gossip. Returning to his West Egg bungalow, Nick sits on an abandoned grass roller in his yard and observes Gatsby standing alone on his lawn, arms outstretched toward a distant green light across the bay, trembling before vanishing into the shadows.

structure.title: II
structure.summary: On a summer Sunday afternoon, Nick Carraway travels by train with Tom Buchanan to the valley of ashes, where Tom forcibly introduces him to Myrtle Wilson at her husband George B. Wilson’s run-down garage; the group then journeys to New York by taxi, with Myrtle riding separately on the train, and stops at a newsstand where she purchases a ten-dollar Airedale puppy. They arrive at Myrtle’s cluttered rented apartment on the top floor of a building at 158th Street, where she hosts a rowdy gathering with her sister Catherine and the McKees, serving whisky and adopting a haughty persona in her cream-coloured chiffon dress, while a blurred photograph falsely identified as her mother hangs on the wall; as alcohol fuels the evening, Myrtle recounts meeting Tom on a train, denounces George as unworthy, and falsely claims Daisy prevents their divorce because she is Catholic, until Myrtle defiantly shouts Daisy’s name—prompting Tom to brutally break her nose, triggering chaos as women scramble with towels, blood stains the bathroom floor and Town Tattle over Versailles tapestry, and Mr. McKee awakens dazed before leaving without speaking; overwhelmed, Nick departs with McKee in the elevator and later wakes asleep on a bench at Pennsylvania Station, waiting for the four o’clock train.

structure.title: III
structure.summary: The chapter opens with Nick Carraway receiving a formal invitation from Jay Gatsby and arriving at Gatsby’s opulent Long Island mansion on a Saturday evening shortly after seven, where a massive party is in full swing with guests arriving by Rolls-Royce and station wagon, swimming at the beach, and being served lavish food and cocktails by eight servants; amid colored garden lights and orchestral music, rumors circulate about Gatsby’s mysterious past—including claims he killed a man or was a German spy—yet he remains absent until midnight, when Nick Carraway finally encounters him at a table, revealing himself with an unnervingly reassuring smile and inviting Nick Carraway to fly in a hydroplane the next morning; as the party descends into chaos with champagne-fueled tears, marital fights, a drunken chorus girl collapsing mid-song, and a new coupé crashing into a wall with its passenger bewilderedly asking for a gas station, Nick Carraway learns from Jordan Baker that she doubts Gatsby’s claim of attending Oxford, and later observes Gatsby standing alone on the porch as guests depart, while outside the wrecked car sits abandoned under the moonlight; between these events, Nick Carraway reflects on his daily life in New York—working at the Probity Trust, lunching with clerks in crowded restaurants, studying investments at the Yale Club’s library at night, and walking home past the old Murray Hill Hotel to Pennsylvania Station—where he reconnects with Jordan, recalling her dishonesty over a damaged borrowed car and a golf tournament scandal, feeling fleeting attraction but restrained by moral codes and unresolved emotional ties to a woman back home to whom he still writes 'Love, Nick'.

structure.title: IV
structure.summary: On a Sunday morning, Gatsby’s mansion hosts a chaotic, extravagant party attended by a vast array of guests from East Egg, West Egg, and New York, arriving by car, including scandalous figures like Snell, who was run over on the gravel drive, and eccentric regulars such as Klipspringer and Benny McClenahan with his interchangeable girls; guests gossip wildly about Gatsby’s alleged crimes and connections to the devil and Von Hindenburg, while Nick Carraway recalls names from a deteriorating 1922 timetable. Later that July, Gatsby arrives at Nick Carraway’s door in his cream-colored car with a three-noted horn, invites him to lunch, and during the drive recounts an elaborate life story—claiming inheritance from wealthy San Francisco parents, education at Oxford, European travels, wartime heroism in the Argonne Forest, and receipt of the Montenegrin 'Orderi di Danilo' for valor, producing physical proof that momentarily convinces Nick Carraway; he reveals he wants Nick Carraway to arrange a meeting with Jordan Baker regarding an undisclosed matter. At noon in a cellar restaurant on Forty-second Street, Gatsby introduces Nick Carraway to Meyer Wolfsheim, who describes in vivid detail the murder of Rosy Rosenthal and claims to have known Gatsby since after the war, praising his discretion and breeding; Gatsby abruptly leaves to make a phone call, and upon returning, becomes visibly embarrassed when introduced to Tom Buchanan and vanishes. In a flashback, Jordan Baker recalls encountering Daisy Fay with Lieutenant Gatsby in Louisville in 1917, leading to Daisy’s family conflict and eventual marriage to Tom Buchanan in 1919 with a $350,000 pearl necklace, during which she was found drunk on the eve of her wedding clutching a letter; years later, in 1922, Jordan mentions Gatsby’s name to Daisy, triggering her emotional recognition of him as the officer from her white roadster. Finally, at twilight, Jordan reveals to Nick Carraway that Gatsby bought his mansion solely to be across the bay from Daisy and wants Nick Carraway to invite Daisy for tea so he can visit casually, having feared offending Nick Carraway and knowing little about Tom beyond reading Chicago papers; Nick Carraway is moved by the quiet desperation behind this modest request after five years of elaborate preparation, and as they ride through Central Park, his focus shifts to Jordan.

structure.title: V
structure.summary: On a rainy night in West Egg, Nick returns home to find Gatsby’s mansion brilliantly lit but eerily silent; Gatsby, unusually anxious, suggests an impromptu trip to Coney Island or a swim, which Nick declines. The next day, Nick agrees to invite Daisy for tea, triggering Gatsby’s obsessive preparations: he hires a gardener to cut Nick’s lawn, inquires about Nick’s income, and tentatively offers him a side business. On the day of the tea, heavy rain floods the neighborhood; Gatsby arrives early in a white suit, visibly trembling, and nearly knocks over a mantelpiece clock when Daisy arrives by large open car with her chauffeur Ferdie. The reunion is initially strained until Daisy’s emotional tears and Gatsby’s radiant transformation signal a quiet reconciliation. After the rain clears, Gatsby joyfully invites Daisy to tour his mansion, entering through the big postern gate, where she admires the feudal silhouette, gardens scented with jonquils, hawthorn, plum blossoms, and kiss-me-at-the-gate, but notes the eerie silence. Gatsby leads her through opulent rooms—including Marie Antoinette music-rooms and Restoration Salons—revealing hidden figures like Mr. Klipspringer doing liver exercises in pyjamas, before displaying his towering stacks of imported shirts, which overwhelm Daisy into sobbing. As rain resumes, Gatsby points out the green light at Daisy’s dock, now diminished in symbolic power, and shows her photographs of Dan Cody and his youthful self in yachting gear; he abruptly ends a phone call about a 'small town' misunderstanding and presents her with clippings about herself. Gatsby summons Klipspringer to play piano poorly in the music room, lights Daisy’s cigarette, and sits with her in near darkness as thunder rolls and West Egg lights up with evening trains returning from New York. Nick observes Gatsby’s growing bewilderment, sensing his idealized vision of Daisy has outgrown reality, and departs as Gatsby and Daisy are utterly absorbed in each other, no longer acknowledging him.

structure.title: VI
characters_present: The woman in the brown riding-habit
structure.summary: The chapter opens with a New York reporter arriving on foot at Gatsby’s mansion, confused by vague rumors of Gatsby’s prominence, prompting a reflection on James Gatz’s transformation into Jay Gatsby at age seventeen when he rowed out to Dan Cody’s yacht anchored in Little Girl Bay on Lake Superior; Gatsby spent five years traveling with Cody across three circumnavigations of the continent, serving in multiple roles and absorbing refined habits while avoiding alcohol after witnessing Cody’s drunken excesses, only to be cheated out of his $25,000 inheritance by Ella Kaye after Cody’s death, yet retaining the identity he forged. Later, after a weeks-long absence, Nick Carraway visits Gatsby’s mansion on a Sunday afternoon and is startled when Tom Buchanan, Mr. Sloane, and a woman in a brown riding-habit arrive on horseback; Gatsby, visibly nervous, insists they stay for drinks and supper, but their cold dismissal is made clear when Sloane subtly blocks Gatsby’s acceptance of the woman’s dinner invitation, leaving him excluded. That week, Tom and Daisy attend Gatsby’s party, where Daisy is both fascinated and appalled by West Egg’s vulgarity; after dancing with her, Gatsby confides in Nick Carraway that Daisy didn’t enjoy the evening and insists he can repeat the past—making her declare she never loved Tom so they can return to Louisville and marry as before—despite Nick Carraway’s warning that the past cannot be repeated, which Gatsby angrily rejects.

structure.title: VII
structure.summary: On the hottest day of summer, Nick arrives by train at the Buchanans’ house to find Gatsby waiting; Gatsby has dismissed his original servants and replaced them with associates of Meyer Wolfsheim to conceal Daisy’s afternoon visits. During lunch, Daisy openly kisses Gatsby and declares her love, shocking Tom, who then challenges Gatsby’s claims of Oxford education and mocks his pink suit. The group departs for New York in two cars—Tom insists Gatsby drive his coupé while he takes Gatsby’s car, forcing Daisy to ride with Gatsby. After stopping at Wilson’s garage in the valley of ashes, where a sick and emotionally shattered George Wilson reveals he plans to take Myrtle away, the party proceeds to the Plaza Hotel in Manhattan. There, a volatile confrontation erupts: Tom exposes Gatsby’s bootlegging ties to Wolfsheim and his criminal past in drugstores, while Daisy, under pressure, first claims she never loved Tom, then breaks down admitting she once loved both men. Tom orders Daisy and Gatsby to leave together in Gatsby’s car, ending the emotional battle. Later, Myrtle Wilson is struck and killed by a speeding yellow car that does not stop; Michaelis discovers her body under a swinging yellow bulb after hearing her shout angrily from downstairs. Tom and Nick arrive at the scene, where Tom denies owning or driving the yellow car, claiming his own is blue, and flees in distress, calling the driver a coward. That night, Gatsby reveals to Nick he has been waiting outside the Buchanan house all night to protect Daisy, insisting he will take blame for the accident—Daisy was driving, and Myrtle ran toward them. Nick secretly observes Daisy and Tom in the kitchen, calmly eating together, confirming their reconciliation. Gatsby remains standing in the moonlight, unaware his vigil is futile.

structure.title: VIII
structure.summary: At dawn on Long Island, Nick Carraway rushes to Gatsby’s mansion after hearing a taxi arrive, finding Gatsby dejected after waiting all night for Daisy to appear at her window; they search the dusty, opulent house for cigarettes and speak on the French windows of the drawing-room, where Nick Carraway urges Gatsby to flee to Atlantic City or Montreal to avoid being linked to Myrtle Wilson’s death, but Gatsby refuses, clinging to the belief that Daisy will choose him. He recounts his youthful romance with Daisy at Camp Taylor, admitting he misled her into believing he was wealthy, and describes their final afternoon together before he left for war—marked by silent tenderness and unspoken devotion. After being mistakenly sent to Oxford instead of returning home, Gatsby learned through a letter that Daisy had married Tom Buchanan, a decision anchored by his social standing and wealth; upon returning penniless to Louisville, Gatsby walked the streets they once knew, desperately trying to reclaim memories of her as the train pulled away. Later, after breakfast on the porch, Gatsby reveals he has never used his pool all summer, and Nick Carraway, moved, declares Gatsby worth more than Daisy and Tom combined, receiving a radiant smile in return. Meanwhile, George Wilson, consumed by grief and delusion after Myrtle’s death, discovers her bruised face and a new dog-leash, concluding her lover murdered her; he travels on foot to Port Roosevelt and Gad’s Hill, buys a sandwich and coffee, vanishes for hours possibly searching for the yellow car, and arrives in West Egg asking for Gatsby’s house. At two p.m., Gatsby puts on his bathing suit, retrieves a pneumatic mattress from the garage, instructs the butler to bring calls to him by the pool, and forbids moving the damaged car; the butler waits until four a.m. for a call that never comes. Gunshots are heard, and Nick Carraway finds Gatsby’s body floating in the pool with the mattress drifting nearby, while the gardener later discovers Wilson’s body in the grass. Nick Carraway, meanwhile, is jolted awake by Jordan Baker’s cold, accusatory phone call from Hempstead, refusing to meet her despite her request, and after four failed attempts to reach Gatsby’s line—reserved for a Detroit call—he marks the 3:50 train and sits in thought.

structure.title: IX
structure.summary: Following Gatsby’s death, Nick Carraway is overwhelmed by the media frenzy at the mansion, where police and reporters sensationalize the tragedy, while Catherine denies Myrtle’s affair with Gatsby and Daisy and Tom vanish without a trace. Nick Carraway’s attempts to contact Wolfshiem and Daisy fail, culminating in a cold letter from Wolfshiem and a mistaken long-distance call about a bond scandal that forces him to announce Gatsby’s death. On the third day, Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives by train from Minnesota, visibly frail and bundled in a cheap ulster, expressing grief and later pride as he shows a photograph of Gatsby’s house and an old copy of Hopalong Cassidy with Gatsby’s youthful self-improvement schedule; despite Nick Carraway’s efforts, only Gatz and a Lutheran minister attend the funeral, as Klipspringer calls for his tennis shoes and Wolfshiem refuses to come, citing his rule against involvement after death. In a heavy drizzle, a procession of three cars — motor hearse, limousine with Gatz and the minister, and Gatsby’s station wagon with servants and the postman — reaches the cemetery, where the man with owl-eyed glasses, whom Nick Carraway doesn’t know by name, appears unexpectedly, wipes rain from his glasses over Gatsby’s grave, murmurs 'Amen to that' after a quiet prayer, and laments that hundreds once attended Gatsby’s parties but now none came, calling him 'the poor son-of-a-bitch.' Nick Carraway later recalls his train journeys to the Midwest, feeling a profound connection to its winter landscapes, and reflects that he, Gatsby, Daisy, Tom, and Jordan are all Westerners out of place in the East, symbolized by a haunting El Greco-esque vision of West Egg where a drunken woman lies ignored on a stretcher. He meets Jordan Baker, who reveals she is engaged to another man; they exchange bitter words about dishonesty and carelessness, ending with his declaration that at thirty he refuses to call dishonesty honor. Finally, he encounters Tom Buchanan on Fifth Avenue, who admits he told Wilson Gatsby owned the car that killed Myrtle, justifying it as necessary despite Gatsby’s moral failings, and tearfully recalls crying over dog biscuits in his abandoned flat; Nick Carraway shakes Tom’s hand, seeing him as a child of careless privilege, before visiting Gatsby’s abandoned house one last time at night, erasing an obscene word on the steps, walking to the beach, and reflecting on the Dutch sailors’ first view of the island and Gatsby’s futile dream symbolized by the green light — ending with the meditation that 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.'

plot_summary.plot_summary:
Nick Carraway, a young Midwesterner seeking opportunity in the East, moves to West Egg in the summer of 1922 and becomes entangled in the lives of his wealthy cousin Daisy Buchanan and her husband Tom, whose marriage is strained by infidelity and moral decay. Through Daisy, Nick meets the enigmatic Jordan Baker, and through their social circles, he is drawn into the orbit of Jay Gatsby, his mysterious neighbor whose lavish parties mask a solitary obsession: rekindling a long-lost romance with Daisy. Gatsby, once James Gatz, has reinvented himself entirely—building wealth through illicit means, acquiring an opulent mansion across the bay from Daisy, and accumulating symbols of status—all to win back the woman he loved five years prior. Nick, moved by Gatsby’s quiet idealism, agrees to facilitate a reunion between Gatsby and Daisy, reigniting a fragile connection that seems to revive Gatsby’s hope.

As Gatsby and Daisy rekindle their affair, tensions escalate between Gatsby and Tom, culminating in a dramatic confrontation at the Plaza Hotel in Manhattan. Tom exposes Gatsby’s criminal ties to Meyer Wolfsheim and undermines his fabricated aristocratic past, while Daisy, overwhelmed, admits she once loved both men but ultimately cannot abandon her life with Tom. That same day, Myrtle Wilson, Tom’s mistress, is killed by a speeding yellow car—driven by Daisy, though Gatsby takes full blame to protect her. In the aftermath, George Wilson, Myrtle’s grieving husband, is manipulated by Tom into believing Gatsby was both Myrtle’s lover and her murderer. Meanwhile, Nick watches helplessly as Gatsby clings to his dream, waiting outside Daisy’s house for a call that never comes, convinced she will choose him despite the chaos he has inherited.

After Gatsby is shot and killed by Wilson in his pool, Nick is left to organize a funeral amid the cold indifference of Gatsby’s former guests and the silence of Daisy and Tom, who vanish without a trace. Only Gatsby’s father, Henry C. Gatz, arrives to mourn, revealing the boyish ambition behind the man—his self-improvement schedule, his reverence for Dan Cody, and his unwavering belief in self-reinvention. As Nick reflects on the emptiness of the East and the moral bankruptcy of its elite, he realizes Gatsby’s tragedy was not his crime or his wealth, but his faith in a dream that had already faded. In the novel’s final moments, Nick visits Gatsby’s abandoned mansion and stands on the beach, gazing at the green light across the bay—a symbol of hope now irretrievably lost—and meditates on the human tendency to strive against the current of time, forever pulled back into the past.
